dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 1
dialogue_entries.text: Carl had been having secret fitness sessions and he'd been to a club where drugs were sold. Well, it doesn't look good. And if Jojo did go to prison, his face would not be pretty for much longer.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 2
dialogue_entries.text: No, we've got away with it so far. If we just keep going, the police may not see anything suspicious.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 3
dialogue_entries.text: A fit, healthy young man who suddenly drops down dead, and your grandson was walking in the woods at the time.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 2
dialogue_entries.text: No, not Jojo. He never had to fly. They couldn't possibly... What's the matter? Please don't blame yourself. I'm sorry if I upset you, and honestly... I've had a lovely time. Joe, Joe, my love. You're not going to believe what your granny's been up to.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 3
dialogue_entries.text: Do you think she'll actually go to prison?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 1
dialogue_entries.text: I wouldn't have thought so. When do you think how long it takes to bring a case to trial and she's at an age where there's no point in buying too large a jar of mayonnaise.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 3
dialogue_entries.text: That's that poor girl I feel sorry for. Scrubbing the bathroom floor till her fingers were bleeding.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 1
dialogue_entries.text: All we can do is take care of people when they're here and hope when they leave they take care of themselves.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 3
dialogue_entries.text: Well, our first weekend and three of our guests survived.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 1
dialogue_entries.text: Yeah, let's concentrate on the positive.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 3
dialogue_entries.text: I've just had a text.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 1
dialogue_entries.text: Oh, anything juicy?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 3
dialogue_entries.text: Possible booking for a wedding party. They want us to look after the bride, bride's mother and about 6 bridesmaids.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 1
dialogue_entries.text: Marvellous. Well, I think this calls for a vodka and tonic. Let's go easy on the tonic.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 3
dialogue_entries.text: In B&B, Buff Men and Bags for Life by David Semple, Brenda was played by Nina Wadia, and Brian by Michael Simpkins, Sue Lorna Laidlaw, Ellie Rose Williams, Carl Adam Sopp, and Jojo was played by Twain Omari Kinch. Music composed and played by A Mnemonic. B&B was produced by Rosalind Ayres, directed by Martin Jarvis, and is a Jarvis and Ayres production.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 4
dialogue_entries.text: BBC News at 3 o'clock. Jersey's assisted dying law has been granted royal assent, making it the first part of the British Isles where it will be legalised. Jersey's States Assembly passed its draft assisted dying law earlier this year. Officials say the law will come into force in the coming days and that work will continue to ensure a service can begin late next year. American and Iranian forces have continued to trade strikes with explosions reported near Iran's main nuclear power plant and in the city of Bandar Abbas. Jordan, which hosts US bases, says it's intercepted 8 missiles launched from Iran. It's emerged that research projects are to be scaled back across the UK after cutbacks in government spending plans. The research includes the hunt for new cancer treatments and the design of improved batteries. Our science correspondent Pallab Ghosh has the details. The government's research agency, UKRI, says it has had to cut back on planned increases in spending to save on cost overruns of more than 160 million pounds in research planned for many physics experiments. The other reason is that the agency is prioritising areas that will create new companies and jobs and so boost Britain's economy. The savings are being mostly made at UKRI's research labs across the UK, which build particle accelerators and telescopes for instruments and work on a range of projects from fighting cancer to developing new materials. The Northern Ireland Secretary, Hilary Benn, has condemned the placing of a model of a mosque on top of a bonfire in County Tyrone as a sickening and cowardly act of intimidation. Bonfires are lit annually in Northern Ireland for the 12th of July, the main date in the Unionist parading season. And the desert rain frog, which became an internet sensation because of the squeaky noise it makes, has been added to the UN's red list of threatened species. It's found only in a narrow stretch of coastal sand dunes in southern Africa, which conservationists say is under threat from development. BBC News.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Kim Cattrall
dialogue_entries.text: Central Intelligence, the story of the CIA from the inside out.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 4
dialogue_entries.text: I've got to make the right call here.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Kim Cattrall
dialogue_entries.text: It's 1964 and President Lyndon B Johnson is in the White House.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 6
dialogue_entries.text: I don't want to start a world war, but I don't want to hand the communies a victory either.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Kim Cattrall
dialogue_entries.text: In the years that follow, the CIA is put to the test.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 7
dialogue_entries.text: I'm sending a helicopter. It's already on its way to pick up your body.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Kim Cattrall
dialogue_entries.text: Starring Kelsey Grammer, Johnny Flynn, David Duchovny, and me, Kim Cattrall.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 7
dialogue_entries.text: Your reputation precedes you.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Kim Cattrall
dialogue_entries.text: The new series of Central Intelligence begins tomorrow afternoon at 2.15 on Radio 4 and BBC Sounds.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 4
dialogue_entries.text: Sue Mitchell and Rob Laurie recently tracked down Tuana Jamal, one of the most prolific people smugglers in recent history, who'd previously been arrested in France but was living and working in the UK. The investigation was carried out for Radio 4's intrigue series To Catch a King, and they found Jamal ahead of the police or the Home Office. In feedback this afternoon, we'll explore how journalists interact with authorities to uncover serious crimes. We'll also return to the subject of BBC cuts and a discussion about how they might affect the BBC's relationship with the public. Feedback is in 30 minutes. But first we'll join Martha Carney to begin a new series of This Natural Life.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: This is such a lovely piece of woodland. in Surrey in a place that feels very wild, but actually a lot of it was planted as a passion project by my guest for this natural life, Dame Judy Dench, as well as that stunning acting career, of course. Her passion has been trees ever since she was a little girl. Now 91, that passion is as strong as ever. And Judy, this is obviously a very special place for you.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: It is, Martha, because when we came here over 40 years ago, Michael and I just decided, because of our love of trees and things, that we would plant trees whenever we could and where we could and where we thought was correct and suitable. And so we now, I plant trees to friends who have died. And so they're very near me, which is extremely nice.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Who are we surrounded by?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: We're surrounded by Michael Gambon over there. And we're surrounded by Eddie Corlekundus and Stephen Hanley. And let me think, who else? Robert Hardy, who, as you probably know, was one of the only men who could draw a longbow. And when the Mary Rose was brought up, The Tudor wreck. Yes, he was one of the only people who could do it. So his tree came from a tree under which the Magna Carta was signed.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: That's amazing.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes, it's nice, isn't it? He'd like that, I think.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: So if I'd come here 40 years ago, when you and your late husband, the actor Michael Williams, first came here, would there have been far fewer trees?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes, I think there were. I mean, There were quite a lot of trees, but I think nothing like now. But we just loved it and it was a very kind of woodland setting then, but we've made it more woodland, I think, hopefully.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: And such a variety of trees, aren't there? Do you have a favourite species?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: I don't really. I've got a lot of cherry trees, lots of cherry trees. And I've got a wonderful... wonderful crab apple tree, which is to Maggie Smith. She liked that very much. And the first fruit that came out on it was the day of her funeral at night, so I had it in my pocket. I thought Mags would like that a lot.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Why did you pick crab apple for her?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: I don't know. I just, you know, I've got the Ginkgo Bilobo for Ediculacundis there. That's the tree that was left standing after Hiroshima. And I've got a tree there for Stephen. I don't know what tree that is, actually. All I know is the blue tits, lovely. For Stephen Hanley, who's a lovely actor who's in Little Night Music. A very tall, pale actor, dancer. And the tree is just so representative of him. And that's how you pick them for the personality of your friend. Yes, in a way.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Why do you think trees are so special to you?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Martha, I can only go back to the fact that when I was a little girl, born and brought up in York with my brothers, I used to, and strange enough still do, get irrationally upset when I saw those huge lorries with trees on them. I, really a little girl, I think four or five, And I've just gone back to that all the time. And so the trees mean such a lot to me. I cannot bear it when I see them or hear the noise of people cutting trees down.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: So you must have been very sad when Sycamore Gap was cut down the famous tree on Hadrian's Hall. As I was, I've walked along there, I couldn't bear it.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: As how many people, people who've been married under it, who've met under it, who've, that's been a focal point of it and such a completely senseless thing to do. But I have, I believe that a nursery garden from Devon came up and collected all the seeds they could very soon after it had happened and took it down. And I was given at Chelsea the year before last, I think. I was given a little Sycamore Gap plant and he's in Meadow Antoninus.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Antoninus, a very good Latin name.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Well, I think he had something to do with Hadrian Antoninus, but I'm not too sure. But anyway, he's there and he looks terrific and taller than me. Not hard. It could be a nettle.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: You were just showing me your calendar, Judi Dench and some tall men. You ambush tall men and ask for a selfie, don't you?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Well, I wouldn't say ambush.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: I would. Just returning to your childhood, do you remember your garden? Do you have strong childhood memories of nature?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes, strong, strong. We had a long, narrow garden with a little hill at the bottom and an old barn on it. And Jeff, my second brother who's an actor long before me, we had owls in the barn and he used to collect the owl pellets and he used to then dissect them and then stick the bones on a piece of card.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: So you could see what the owl had been eating.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: So you could see exactly what he'd been eating. And we used to grow a lot of vegetables and things. And we had a wonderful greenhouse attached to the to the house which had been there, I think long before my daddy bought the house. And we had really great grapes. And the boys used to play cricket in the garden. And they used to be always batting the balls over into the other gardens. And there was a lady called Miss Lazenby, and she never, ever would throw the ball back or give us the balls back. This is a terrible story. And once the boys found a dead rat in the barn, and they parcelled it up, and they said to me, Julie, will you just go round and put this through Miss Lazenby's stool?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: No.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: So I did go and squeeze it through Miss Lazenby's stool. Miss Lazenby was round in about an hour and a half.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Not really surprised.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Saying, Please give us our balls back. We did some message.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: It was a message tied around the dead rack.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes, tied on the dead rack.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: And did they ever get their balls back? Probably not.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: I doubt we ever didn't think we were allowed to play cricket again.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: You obviously had great fun with your brothers. Did you used to play out in the garden, play out in the countryside or?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Cycle, roller skate, swim mostly. We used to cycle. All of us had bikes. My parents and the boys and I. And trend. of theirs and we used to cycle out the castle hard and swim in the lake.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: A perfect place to swim.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Cold, I imagine. Cold, cold and black. Very, very dark lake. But yes, it's where I like to swim.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: We've got a plane coming over. You're quite near. We're in a country idyll, but also quite near Gatwick Airport, so we'll let the planes go by.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes, let them go past.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: And I was reading that one of your very early acting roles has a nature connection.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: You mean my very first acting role, Martha?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: I think it was.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Do people know that rhyme anymore? Four and 20 sailors. Is it sailors or tailors? I've never known. Went to kill a snail. The best man amongst them dares not touch her tail. She put out her horns Something curly cow, run, tailors or sailors run, or she'll catch you all there now. I think it was. And I was the snail. And my Pa, he couldn't make anything, Daddy, made me a huge, out of buckram. Remember what buckram?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Buckram, that's a stiffened, fresh fabric.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes, that's right. He made me this incredible shell. And I was in kind of rompers, and the shell tied round me. And Miss Mebe, who's head of our school, said, Judith, you just crouch down as a snail. And when they say put out your horns, you just do that. That's all you have to do. Fine, absolutely fine. And we rehearsed it. Fine, fine. And then, of course, your parents come or your friends or anything. You've got an audience. And so I was crouching down, waiting, and the audience were all, that's very, very quiet. But immediately there was any kind of reaction, I got up to have a look. And I just hear Miss Mabey, who's the head of school, I remember saying, get down, Judith. First notice I ever had.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Not a very good notice.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: A very naughty notice.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: And I think you also drew on nature as an inspiration when you were at drama school, when you were at the Central, and you had to do a mime, which you completely unprepared for. You made it up on the spare of the moment.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: I'd completely forgotten we had to do it. Walter had asked us to do a mime. And, you know, he said, we'll do the mime now. Julia, would you get... I thought, the mime? Crikey. And so I... Well, it was totally unprepared. I stood, stood and I... walked forward, thinking, what the hell am I going to do? And then I bent down and picked up something and smelt it. And then I looked around. I was still thinking, what am I going to do? And then I walked a bit more. And then I sat down and just looked around and said, well, anyway, I got the most sensational reaction from Walter Hunt. He said, this is exactly what I mean.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: I completely by chance. But you imagined you were in a garden.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: That was the idea. Yes, that's all I could think. Because I sat down on a swing at one point and all the time I was thinking, what else am I going to do? You know, it was completely by chance.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Well, I'd like to explore a bit more of this magical woodland. So perhaps we could walk a bit further down the path and you can show me some more.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Indeed.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: You've got lots of wild garlic, haven't you? And the white flowers are out at the moment.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes, if you want some white garlic, take an armful or a carful.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: And we've come into a different area of the garden now. I think those are that kind of acidy green. I think those are Alexander's. Is this a walk you do regularly?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Well, I do if there's somebody around. Hang on. Because my eyes now are so bad that I, if the ground is uneven, it's a hazard. It's tricky, yeah. But if people are here, I can.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Does that mean, does the fact that your eyesight's got worse, does that mean you have a different relationship with nature? Do you, is it, does sound more important or?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Sound is very important and touch is very important. As long as I can feel the tree, No, I can go up and touch it. What I've missed this year terribly is the fact that I have not seen the bluebells and I believe they were absolutely sensational here and I've missed that this year.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: But I suppose if you get the right bluebells, you do get the smell, don't you? When you're surrounded by bluebells, you can smell.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Do you know, I suppose you can. I've forgotten the smell of a bluebell. That's a terrible thing to say. Never mind.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: I can see just over there behind us, it looks like, well, they're trained plants, but over a couple of, are they boxing hares?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: They are boxing hares. They are beautiful boxing hares that were given to me. And they've been mowed around, so they look, you know, rather as if they belong there in the ring in the middle, having a bit of a bite.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: What kind of wildlife do you have here?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: We have squirrels and we have lots of foxes. And we have ducks. We have ducks which we feed morning and evening. Who else do we have? Oh, we have a lot of deer.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Oh, well, of course, they love the woodland.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes, they love it. And they come in and one walked straight up through the white garden and onto the front lawn the other day.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Eat any of your flower beds, that's what we have. I saw one destroy a bed of my beautiful Aquilegia. It was like a strimmer just went through.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: He took the tops off the white tulips. Can I have a tulip? This tree here, Tony Kirkham, my great friend Tony Kirkham worked at Kew, came down and he told me that this tree here would have been there at the Battle of Waterloo. And we measured it, we had got a tape measure round it and measured it. was so wonderful to do. But I just love it.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Do you know what I'd love us both to do? If we can just go through the wild garlic a little bit and just feel that bark. Yes. Because it's such beautiful, isn't it? Let's feel it.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Be careful. Don't fall over anything or down the rabbit hole. Whoops. Isn't it lovely?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 10
dialogue_entries.text: Oh, such a beautiful thing, isn't it? Isn't it?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: He's seen a few things in his time. And Oak is a family name of ours. That's why Sammy is Samuel Michael Oak.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Your grandson.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 10
dialogue_entries.text: Oh, I just love the feel of this. And as you say, when you think it's been here more than 200 years.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 10
dialogue_entries.text: It's a different way of experiencing nature, isn't it? Yes.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Just going through a lovely art with a, you've got a little clematis growing over it, so delicate.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 10
dialogue_entries.text: Who's this?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Will Shakespeare. He likes it out here, you can see, standing on his stone, Mr Shakespeare thinking up a few more sonnets, hopefully for us all.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: So this is an award you won that you've put on a stone plinth in the garden.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: It's a perfect place for it.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Oh, yes, Tom. Oh. Tom, so this is for Tom Stoppard. Yes. Who died quite recently, didn't he?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: And I can just, I wouldn't know it by sight, but I've just read the label and I think it's a hornbeam.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Oh, yes, hornbeam, that's right.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: I've just planted a couple of hornbeams. And something that I like about planting a tree is when I was doing it, I was thinking, this is not going to be for me. They're not going to get very tall in my lifetime. But it's a way of thinking about yourself in the future, isn't it?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: I quite agree. I quite agree.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: What kind of tree would you have planted for you, do you think? What kind of tree? If somebody decided, if...

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Very, very tall. Something immensely tall I have.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: But the light is so lovely. I think you must be able to feel it on your face, the way it's coming through the trees, the dappled sunshine.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Isn't it lovely? It's lovely. We're coming up to Mike's tree.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 10
dialogue_entries.text: Oh, yes.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: This is Mike, yes, on the little plaque at the bottom. This is for your late husband. So just by planting your hands as you've done on the tree. Does that make you feel a connection in some way?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: I think it should, with all of us too, you know, just to the fact that it's, you know, that wonderful tree, so strong and solid and constant.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Constant. Let's carry on back into the more formal part of the garden. Actually, I'm just going to have to stop because that bird sound is so lovely. I've just got to stop and do something which I love doing, which is just I tried to identify the birds with an app on my phone, which I couldn't really do with many of them without the app. Look, that's a wren and a black cap. And I always love the sound of the wren because for such a small bird, a lot of noise, a lot of noise. And I've been listening, I think, while we've been recording to the chiff-chaff, which is one of the easiest ones, isn't it, to identify. And I suppose with the deterioration in your sight, does the sound of the birds, does that become more precious?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: It absolutely does. Can't do without them. But you've got so many ears. We don't hear anymore. That's the cuckoo. I haven't heard from the whole of the spring.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Do you worry about the state of nature? Do you worry when you can't hear birds like that?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Well, I, you know, there are people who've never heard a cuckoo. And a cuckoo is such an sensual part of saying, gosh, it's spring, it must be spring, listen. It was a completely accepted thing. that you would always hear the cuckoo in the spring.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: And you've done some campaigns, haven't you, where talking about the importance of parks in London, for example, that you think that, you know, this is something that we need to fight to preserve.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: We must have them. I mean, the more building there is, the more we must even it out with spaces, where there are not buildings, and where you can just, you know, be in a space that Changes constantly all around you.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: In the course of all the films that you've made, you must have gone to some amazing locations abroad and in this country.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: We did. Yes, we went to West Wickham to do some of the importance that we'd done on stage at the National. Importance of being earnest, yeah. And a very charming thing happened there because on the gate there, they put for the public the birds that are seen each day. they'll say, 4 swallows and an owl and two chiff-chaffs, things like that. And so we got there one day and it said, 4 swallows and a chiff-chaff and a robin and dainty dainty on her phone.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Sighting of a rare bird. We're by your pond now and this is a great resource for wildlife, isn't it, to have a pond in the garden?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: It's essential. Alas, the water is very low at the moment and it usually runs down and under that bridge and right down into the meadow. But we have to do a bit of pumping, I think, from the well to get it back. But We have a lot of ducks. We've had not so many now. We used to have about 40. They are fed morning and evening. Of course, 40. But there's only a couple around at the moment.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: I think when you first came here, your daughter, Finty, was quite young and I can imagine this must have been a wonderful place for a child.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yes, I think she loved it and her friends. And subsequently, her son absolutely adores it. In fact, it's going to be his birthday in about two, three weeks' time. And he's going to have a silent disco in the meadow.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: I hope you'll be joining in.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Oh, you bet.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: Do you like dancing, don't you?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Dame Judy Dench
dialogue_entries.text: Yeah, I love it.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Martha Carney
dialogue_entries.text: I love that image that you've been dancing wildly in the meadow with your headphones on.
